newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Tax fears shake UK shares, more damage seen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tax fears shake UK shares, more damage seen.

text.p: Speculation that Britain's Labour government could remove tax advantages for pension funds owning equities sent tremors through London's stock market on Monday and analysts warned more damage could be on the way.

The FTSE 100 index of blue-chip shares dropped 42.9 points to 4,740.2 by 1140 GMT after a Financial Times report fuelled existing market concerns that the government's July 2 budget would abolish the 20-percent tax credit on dividend payments claimed by tax-exempt institutions like pension funds and charities.
The newspaper quoted an unnamed senior member of the government as saying the tax break would be scrapped.
"They've been quite good at leaking stuff in advance so far," BZW UK market strategist Steve Wright said. "It seems to be that it's almost a done deal."
Analysts said the FTSE could dive 10 percent if the tax credit was ended, with high-yielding stocks bearing the brunt of the losses as shares become less attractive compared with government bonds.

"In the worst case scenario we could find ourselves flirting with the 4,000 level," said Jeremy Batstone, head of research at NatWest Stockbrokers. "But I would expect a correction rather than a collapse because at that level yields would provide some underpinning."
Robert Buckland, UK strategist at HSBC James Capel, said abolition of the tax credit could drag the market 10 percent lower although some of the damage may already be priced in.
"We have a rule of thumb that the market will be hit by half of what the credit is cut by," Buckland said.

"So if the credit is cut to 10 percent, the market will fall around five percent, or 10 percent if the credit is abolished altogether. But that's the most extreme case if it hasn't been priced in to some extent already."

The worst affected shares would be those which have traditionally been generous with their dividends, analysts say. If the tax credit is removed, the dividend payments of high-yielders will no longer be be so attractive for pension funds.

Utilities and insurers were among the hardest hit on Monday. Compared with an average historic yield of 3.4 percent for the FTSE 100 index, water shares yield 6.3 percent, electricity shares 5.6 percent and insurers 4.8 percent.

"The companies most impacted would be those paying high dividends as a percentage of earnings, and those with poor cash flow and low dividend cover," Batstone said. "Utilities stocks are in the front line."

Buckland said companies with low dividend growth would also be at risk. "The shares which will suffer most are those with high yield but low dividend growth, because if you are buying them for the up-front dividend, you will be disappointed if the credit were to go," he said.

As well as impacting on the institutional demand for shares, ending the tax credit could also hit companies with pension funds, forcing them to top-up the funds from pre-tax profits to prevent them becoming underfunded.

"We've calculated it could knock 1.5 to two percent off corporate earnings, but spread over a few years. So it's not a big deal in that regard, although it will hit some companies more than others," Buckland said.

Analysts say abolishing the tax credit could raise five billion pounds ($8.2 billion) for the government, which faces the dilemma of raising extra tax revenue while honouring its election pledge of keeping income tax rates down.

Labour also wants to end "short termism" in the economy, and some economists say the tax credit causes short-sighted behaviour by encouraging pension funds to pressure companies to pay high dividends at the expense of long-term investment.

But abolition of the credit would face strong opposition from business groups -- the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) and National Association of Pension Funds (NAPF) have both warned the government against such a move. The influential Lex column in the Financial Times added to the warnings on Monday.

"If the goverment rushes down this route, abandoning the promise of a real review (of the corporate tax system), it can wave goodbye to the trust it has so far enjoyed from the business community," the newspaper said. "Its alleged commitment to encouraging investment will also be left in tatters."
($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
